fields.Headline: AI Researchers Issue Urgent Call for International Controls
fields.Body:
In a rare display of cross-company consensus, more than 1,100 AI researchers from the world's leading labs—including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, Microsoft, Mistral, and Thinking Machines—have signed a public statement titled "Pacing the Frontier" on July 28. The signatories include OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki, chief research officer Mark Chen, and co-founders Wojciech Zaremba and John Schulman, as well as Anthropic co-founders Jack Clark, Chris Olah, and Ben Mann. Their core demand: the US government should support the creation of an international mechanism capable of actively controlling frontier AI, particularly by slowing the pace of automated AI research and development when necessary.

The move is striking because OpenAI and Anthropic have been engaged in fierce competition for researchers, corporate clients, and computing power, while also lobbying for divergent AI regulatory frameworks in Washington. The joint appeal signals a shared recognition that the technology's trajectory could pose systemic risks that transcend corporate rivalries. The statement does not specify exact thresholds for intervention, but its focus on "automated AI R&D" points to concerns about AI systems that can recursively improve themselves or generate new AI models without human oversight.

For global investors and China watchers, the initiative underscores a deepening debate about how to govern AI at a time when both the US and China are racing to dominate the field. While the statement targets US policy, any international mechanism would inevitably involve coordination—or confrontation—with China, which has its own ambitious AI development plans and a different regulatory philosophy. The call also highlights growing internal unease within the tech sector about the speed of commercial deployment, which could lead to stricter self-regulation or external constraints that slow product releases and affect business models.
fields.Why It Matters: This unprecedented coalition of AI researchers from competing companies signals that industry insiders view current governance as insufficient, potentially presaging regulatory tightening. For global tech investors, any international control mechanism could disrupt AI development timelines and alter competitive dynamics between US and Chinese AI firms.
fields.Author: ChinaPulse Editorial
fields.Summary: Over 1,100 researchers from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, and other leading AI labs have signed an open statement urging the US government to establish an international mechanism to control frontier AI development, including slowing automated AI research when necessary. The unusual show of unity reflects growing alarm within the industry about the pace of AI advancement.

fields.Headline: China Rejects 'Excess Capacity' Label in New White Paper
fields.Body:
China's Ministry of Commerce on Tuesday published a position paper addressing the so-called excess capacity issue, pushing back against claims that Chinese industries are producing far more than market demand. The document, titled "China's Position on the So-called Excess Capacity Issue," calls for an objective and fact-based discussion, arguing that the narrative has been used to justify trade restrictions.

While the full text was not immediately available, the release marks Beijing's latest effort to counter criticism from the US and Europe, particularly regarding overcapacity in sectors like solar panels, electric vehicles, and steel. Chinese officials have previously argued that capacity utilization figures are often misrepresented and that competitive pricing reflects efficiency rather than subsidy-fueled overproduction.

The move comes as global trade tensions continue to simmer, with the EU and US considering new tariffs on Chinese green-tech products. By issuing a formal position paper, China is signaling its intent to shape the international narrative and resist pressure to curb output, which could lead to further disputes at the WTO.
fields.Why It Matters: Investors in sectors like EVs and solar should expect continued friction as China fights 'excess capacity' accusations. This document may foreshadow retaliatory measures or tariff negotiations, affecting supply chains and pricing globally.
fields.Author: ChinaPulse Editorial
fields.Summary: China's Ministry of Commerce released a document titled 'China's Position on the So-called Excess Capacity Issue' on Tuesday, calling for an objective assessment. The paper argues that the 'excess capacity' narrative is misleading and driven by protectionism.

fields.Headline: Laopu Gold Sales Surge 60% as Stock Halves from Peak
fields.Body:
Laopu Gold, a premium Chinese jeweler, is experiencing a tale of two markets. On one hand, its physical stores remain crowded—on July 23, the first day of Qixi Festival pre-sales, customers lined up before the Beijing SKP opened, with one source noting that "SKP's performance now depends on Laopu." Yet on the other hand, the company's stock has fallen more than 50% from its July 2025 peak amid a broad gold price correction and a weak Q2 consumer environment.

On July 27, Laopu released a positive profit alert for H1 2026, reporting sales of RMB 22.7–23.35 billion, up 60–65% YoY, and net profit of RMB 4.31–4.36 billion, up 83–85%. According to Frost & Sullivan, Laopu has ranked first in store efficiency among luxury brands for 18 consecutive months. The data show that even under the "biggest stress test" of deep gold price corrections, high base effects, and weak consumption, the company delivered industry-leading growth.

The divergence between strong fundamentals and weak equity performance raises questions about investor sentiment. Gold price volatility this year has been "epic," with prices falling back to 2025 levels, and broader consumer weakness in Q2 may have spooked markets. However, Laopu's ability to maintain premium pricing and foot traffic suggests its brand intangible remains resilient, even if short-term macroeconomic headwinds persist.
fields.Why It Matters: Laopu Gold's performance highlights the resilience of luxury consumption among China's wealthy despite economic woes. Investors should watch whether the stock recovers as sentiment stabilizes, and whether other luxury retailers can similarly defy the downturn.
fields.Author: ChinaPulse Editorial
fields.Summary: Laopu Gold reported strong H1 results with sales up ~60% YoY despite a sharp stock decline and volatile gold prices. The luxury jeweler continues to see strong in-store demand at high-end malls like Beijing SKP.

fields.Headline: Japan's Robotics Giants Abandon Full Self-Development to Rejoin Global Race
fields.Body:
For the past two years, the global embodied intelligence sector has been dominated by Chinese and US companies, with China accounting for ~85% of humanoid robot shipments in 2025. Japan, once the undisputed leader in industrial robotics, has been conspicuously absent. A July 23 teardown by Nikkei xTECH of Unitree's G1 robot acknowledged that Japan's industrial advantages have eroded, and Japan now holds only ~10% of the service robot market despite 70% of the industrial robot market.

Now, Japanese giants are pivoting. In May, FANUC announced a deep partnership with Google, using its Gemini AI to enable multi-robot collaboration driven by natural language, sending its stock up nearly 14% after hours. It then deepened its partnership with Nvidia. On May 22, Kawasaki Heavy Industries established a physical AI R&D center in Silicon Valley. Meanwhile, SoftBank CEO Masayoshi Son declared his ambition to build "the world's number one AI robot company" at the June shareholder meeting.

The shift from a full self-development model to a collaborative one marks a strategic realignment. By leveraging US tech giants' AI platforms, Japanese firms aim to accelerate time-to-market. This trend mirrors similar moves in the auto and electronics industries, where Japanese companies have increasingly partnered with foreign tech leaders to stay competitive.
fields.Why It Matters: The abandonment of full self-development by Japanese robotics leaders signals a new phase in the global AI robotics race, with implications for supply chains and partnerships. China's dominance may face renewed competition as Japan leverages US AI stacks.
fields.Author: ChinaPulse Editorial
fields.Summary: FANUC, Kawasaki Heavy, and SoftBank are shifting strategies, partnering with Google, Nvidia, and others as Japanese firms cede ground to Chinese rivals in humanoid robotics. The move signals a "co-opetition" approach to catch up.

fields.Headline: Volvo China's D-Class Sedan Project Deepens Geely Integration
fields.Body:
According to multiple industry sources, Volvo is preparing to launch a new D-class ultra-luxury flagship sedan with the internal codename "561." The car is positioned to compete with the Hongqi S800 and will surpass the current S90 as Volvo's highest-spec sedan. The project is being spearheaded by Duan Jianjun, who took over as Volvo China president and CEO less than 100 days ago after a 13-year stint at Beijing Benz, where he built the S-Class and Maybach into dominant D-segment players in China.

The "561" project is Volvo's first-ever D-class executive sedan in its 100-year history, and also the first for Geely Group in its 40-year history. The car will be a China-exclusive model. Volvo China will define the product, set safety standards, and handle certification, while Geely's Chinese R&D team will manage three-electric (battery, motor, electronics) development, vehicle engineering, and supply chain.

Volvo's global CEO hinted at two new electric vehicles to be revealed in early autumn during a Q2 earnings call on July 17, though whether "561" is among them remains unclear. The project represents a major step in Volvo's localization and integration with Geely, leveraging Geely's scale while preserving Volvo's brand identity.
fields.Why It Matters: The '561' project shows how foreign brands in China increasingly rely on local partnerships to compete in premium segments. For investors, it illustrates the deepening of Geely's influence over Volvo and the growing importance of China-specific models.
fields.Author: ChinaPulse Editorial
fields.Summary: Volvo is developing a D-class ultra-luxury sedan (codename '561') for China, its first-ever executive sedan. The car will use a co-development model with Geely, with Volvo China handling product definition and safety, while Geely manages engineering and supply chain.

fields.Headline: Hong Kong Shopping Festival Targets Southeast Asia
fields.Body:
The Hong Kong Shopping Festival, an annual e-commerce event designed to support the city's small and medium-sized enterprises, is venturing into Southeast Asia for the first time. According to the South China Morning Post, the Trade Development Council (TDC) announced on Tuesday that the third edition, launching next month, will include editions in Singapore and Malaysia, with plans to add other ASEAN countries in the future.

The festival has attracted a record number of local Hong Kong brands this year across both its mainland China and ASEAN editions, signaling growing appetite for Hong Kong consumer goods among regional buyers. The expansion reflects Hong Kong's strategic push to diversify its retail outreach beyond mainland China, leveraging the city's reputation for quality and trust.

For global brands and investors, the move underscores ASEAN's rising importance as a consumer market and Hong Kong's role as a gateway. However, competition from regional e-commerce giants like Shopee and Lazada, as well as local brands in Singapore and Malaysia, will pose challenges. The festival's success in these markets could inform broader retail strategies for the region.
fields.Why It Matters: Hong Kong's retail push into ASEAN offers a test case for cross-border e-commerce among SMEs. Brands watching the festival's performance in Singapore and Malaysia will gain insights into consumer preferences and logistical viability in Southeast Asia.
fields.Author: ChinaPulse Editorial
fields.Summary: The Hong Kong Shopping Festival, organized by the Trade Development Council, will expand into ASEAN for the first time via Singapore and Malaysia. The third edition launches next month with a record number of local brands.

fields.Headline: Trip.com Q1 Revenue Hits $22.4B, Warns of Q2 Slowdown
fields.Body:
Trip.com Group, China's largest online travel agency, reported net revenue of 16.2 billion yuan (approximately $22.4 billion) in the first quarter of 2026, according to TravelDaily. The strong start to the year was driven by a robust rebound in both domestic and international travel demand, particularly during the Chinese New Year holiday period.

However, the company's guidance for the second quarter indicates a significant slowdown. According to the report, Trip.com expects Q2 revenue growth to decelerate markedly compared to Q1, reflecting cautious consumer spending, a weaker macroeconomic environment, and intensifying competition from domestic rivals such as Meituan and Fliggy.

For global investors, Trip.com's trajectory serves as a bellwether for China's travel recovery. The Q1 numbers confirm sustained demand, but the Q2 warning suggests that the post-pandemic travel boom may be plateauing. The company's ability to navigate margin pressures and maintain market share will be critical in the coming quarters.
fields.Why It Matters: Trip.com's Q1 results highlight the resilience of China's travel sector, but the Q2 slowdown signals caution. Investors and travel brands should watch for weakening consumer sentiment and adjust their China exposure accordingly.
fields.Author: ChinaPulse Editorial
fields.Summary: Trip.com Group reported net revenue of 16.2 billion yuan ($22.4 billion) for Q1 2026, but forecasts a sharp deceleration in Q2 growth amid global economic headwinds and shifting travel patterns.

fields.Headline: Chinese Tourist Numbers to Japan Plunge Nearly 60%
fields.Body:
Japan's tourism industry is reeling from a nearly 60% drop in Chinese tourist arrivals, according to Pinchain. The decline, which has accelerated in recent months, comes as a severe setback for a sector that had pinned hopes on a strong rebound from Chinese travelers post-pandemic.

Multiple factors are at play. Geopolitical strains between China and Japan, including disputes over the East China Sea and historical issues, have dampened Chinese appetite for travel to Japan. Additionally, the yen's prolonged weakness has made Japan more expensive for Chinese tourists, while Japan's visa restrictions have become more stringent following a surge in overstayers.

The impact on Japan's retail, hospitality, and luxury sectors is pronounced. Chinese tourists were historically among the biggest spenders, particularly on cosmetics, electronics, and duty-free goods. A prolonged slump could force Japanese businesses to pivot toward other source markets, such as Southeast Asia or the Middle East, but volumes are unlikely to compensate fully.
fields.Why It Matters: The collapse in Chinese tourism to Japan illustrates how political and economic factors can rapidly reshape travel flows. Hotel chains, luxury retailers, and airlines should reassess their exposure to Chinese outbound travel to Japan and diversify marketing strategies.
fields.Author: ChinaPulse Editorial
fields.Summary: Chinese visitor arrivals in Japan have slumped by nearly 60%, dealing a heavy blow to Japan's tourism sector. The sharp decline is attributed to geopolitical tensions, a weak yen, and stricter visa policies.

fields.Headline: Russian Tourists Flock to China for Scenery and Traditional Medicine
fields.Body:
China's summer tourism is receiving an unexpected boost from Russian visitors, according to Pinchain. The report highlights that Russian tourists are increasingly drawn to Chinese destinations known for natural beauty, such as the mountainous regions of Sichuan and Yunnan, as well as wellness offerings like traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) treatments.

This trend is partly driven by easier visa procedures for Russian nationals and competitive pricing compared to European destinations. The Chinese government has been promoting inbound tourism as part of its post-pandemic recovery strategy, and Russia has emerged as a key growth market, with direct flights added to several cities.

For Chinese tourism operators, the influx of Russian visitors provides a welcome diversification after the sharp decline in Western tourists. TCM clinics and resorts are marketing packages that combine sightseeing with acupuncture, herbal remedies, and tai chi classes, appealing to Russians' growing interest in holistic health. However, language barriers and differences in service expectations remain challenges.
fields.Why It Matters: The rise in Russian tourism to China underscores shifting source market dynamics. Brands in wellness, hospitality, and TCM should consider targeting Russian consumers, while tourism boards may invest in Russian-language marketing and tailored experiences.
fields.Author: ChinaPulse Editorial
fields.Summary: A growing number of Russian tourists are choosing China as a summer destination, attracted by scenic landscapes and traditional Chinese medicine services. This trend highlights a shift in source markets for China's inbound tourism.

fields.Headline: Moonshot AI's K3 Model Challenges DeepSeek with Novel Architecture
fields.Body:
Moonshot AI has published a detailed 47-page technical report on its K3 model, directly challenging rival DeepSeek, according to Pandaily. The report introduces several architectural breakthroughs: KDA+Gated MLA hybrid attention for efficient long-context processing, AttnRes for cross-layer retrieval, Stable LatentMoE with 896 experts to scale model capacity, and a massive reinforcement learning sandbox with 51.2 million parallel environments.

The K3 model appears designed to push the boundaries of scaling laws, with two distinct axes: one for model parameters and another for training compute via reinforcement learning. This dual-axis scaling could redefine how frontier models are developed, moving beyond simple parameter scaling toward more sophisticated training regimes.

For the global AI community, Moonshot's K3 represents a serious contender in the large language model race, particularly in the Chinese ecosystem. The emphasis on reinforcement learning and multi-agent sandboxes suggests a focus on reasoning and real-world simulation, areas where DeepSeek has also been investing. Competition between the two labs is likely to accelerate innovation but also raise the bar for compute and data requirements.
fields.Why It Matters: Moonshot AI's K3 introduces architectural innovations that could impact the cost and performance of frontier AI models. Investors and tech leaders should monitor how these designs influence the competitive landscape, particularly in China's AI sector where both Moonshot and DeepSeek are key players.
fields.Author: ChinaPulse Editorial
fields.Summary: Moonshot AI's 47-page K3 technical report reveals innovations including KDA+Gated MLA attention, LatentMoE with 896 experts, and 51.2 million reinforcement learning sandboxes, signaling a new frontier in AI development.
